It prepares a Renewal Quote when the customer expresses intent, negotiates terms, and develops a Retention Plan if the renewal is at risk. Non-standard terms are escalated rather than introduced on the spot.

**A Renewal Quote follows intent.** Each quote is based on the current Contract and approved pricing; new terms cannot appear without a contract amendment process. The quote is judged on timeliness, accuracy, and the probability that the customer stays.

Name: Sell by Proposal
Documentation:
**A formal request for proposal arrives.** It carries a deadline, evaluation criteria, and submission requirements. Sell by Proposal develops a tailored Proposal that answers the customer's stated needs and sets terms for later contracting. Missing the deadline or failing to address the evaluation criteria means disqualification, so compliance with the request is not optional.

**It builds a compliant response.** The capability reviews the Request for Proposal, develops a solution concept, and drafts the Proposal. It obtains internal approval through a Proposal Summary before submission, and it revises the Proposal when the customer asks for clarification. Competitive Insight must be legally obtained and sourced; unsourced insight is discarded.

**The Proposal answers every mandatory requirement.** The document conforms to the Request for Proposal format, and any deviation causes disqualification. After the decision, a Win/Loss Analysis records why the bid succeeded or failed, feeding the next proposal.

Name: Sell on Standard Terms
Documentation:
**A customer requests a standard offering.** The request names the product or service and the quantity. Sell on Standard Terms turns that interest into an order without bespoke negotiation. It quotes the price from the approved Pricing List, applies the current Standard Terms Template, and issues a Standard Terms Quote. A delayed or mispriced quote sends the customer elsewhere or sells at a loss, so the work runs on version-controlled terms and approved prices only.

**It links customer interest to fulfilment.** The capability receives Customer Inquiry, Standard Terms Template from legal, and Pricing List from finance. It validates customer eligibility, confirms the order when the customer accepts, and releases a Sales Order for fulfilment. Orders outside standard parameters are rejected. Off-list pricing requires documented approval.

**A Standard Terms Quote is issued.** The quote uses the current Standard Terms Template and the approved Pricing List. It is issued when the customer selects an offering, and it records both the term version and the price accuracy needed to convert interest into an order.

Name: Source Returns
Documentation:
**A defective input triggers return checks.** When a defective or incorrect input is identified, a Return Request arrives. Source Returns verifies it against the original Purchase Order and Goods Receipt, and checks the Supply Agreement return terms. The disposition is determined as replace, repair, or refund, and a Return Authorization is issued only when the evidence supports it. This gets defective inputs out of inventory and forces supplier correction.

**Returns stay tied to original purchase.** Source Returns depends on Quality Inspection Results to confirm the defect, and on Supply Agreements for return windows and remedies. It produces Return Shipment Notifications when goods go back, and Corrective Action Requests when the same reason repeats. Credit Note Requests are issued when the remedy is a credit. These connections keep every return traceable to the original transaction.

**A Return Authorization gates dispatch.** When a Return Request matches contract return terms and has traceability to the original Purchase Order and Goods Receipt, a Return Authorization is issued. Only after that is a Return Shipment Notification issued and the goods dispatched. Without that record, nothing leaves the facility back to the supplier.

Name: Source-to-Engineering-Order
Documentation:
**A new design needs non-standard input.** When a new design or prototype requires an input outside standard supply agreements, Source-to-Engineering-Order translates the Engineering Specification into a procurement specification. It identifies supplier candidates, requests quotes and technical samples, and evaluates technical compliance before issuing a Purchase Order. Technical feasibility replaces price as the primary filter, because there is no purchase history to fall back on.

**Technical reports drive each purchase.** It depends on Engineering Specifications and Engineering Change Notices to define what is needed. Technical Evaluation Reports judge whether a supplier sample meets the specification. If a supplier fails validation, a Supplier Development Request is issued instead of proceeding. Purchase Orders for prototype quantities are issued only after technical acceptance, and Purchase Order Amendments reference the Engineering Change Notice.

**A Technical Acceptance confirms capability.** When a supplied sample passes validation against the Engineering Specification, a Technical Acceptance is issued. That record is the evidence that the supplier meets the design requirements. The Purchase Order for prototype quantity is issued only after it exists.

Name: Source-to-Order
Documentation:
**A customer order sets the clock.** When a customer order arrives with sourced inputs, Source-to-Order extracts its line items and checks each input against Supply Agreements and the Approved Supplier List. If no existing agreement covers it, the work obtains a Supplier Quote. The supplier is selected based on the quote and the order due date, so capacity matches the delivery requirement and pricing is order-specific before commitment.

**Every purchase ties to one order.** Source-to-Order depends on Supply Agreements for terms and the Approved Supplier List for qualified suppliers. It issues Purchase Orders tied to the specific Customer Order. If the customer order changes or cancels, it issues Purchase Order Amendments or Cancellations. Supplier Order Acknowledgments confirm acceptance, and discrepancies between quote and order are resolved before commitment.

**A Purchase Order pins commitment.** After a supplier is selected and the Supplier Quote accepted, a Purchase Order is issued against the Supply Agreement. It carries the exact quantities, specifications, and due date from the customer order. Any later change to the customer order requires a Purchase Order Amendment that records the change reason.

Name: Source-to-Replenish
Documentation:
**Stock below reorder point starts work.** Source-to-Replenish monitors inventory position against reorder points. When stock falls below the reorder point, it calculates how much to order based on the demand forecast and the supplier lead time, selects an Approved Supplier, and issues a Purchase Order. This keeps inventory within policy while avoiding stockouts and excess holding.

**Forecasts and lead times shape orders.** It consumes Replenishment Signals, Inventory Positions, Demand Forecasts, Supply Agreements, Approved Supplier List, and Supplier Performance Reports. Supplier Performance Reports trigger expediting when deliveries are late, and Purchase Orders are adjusted when forecasts change. Stock Transfer Orders rebalance inventory across locations. These connections keep purchasing responsive to actual stock and demand.

**A Purchase Order sets replenishment.** When a Replenishment Signal triggers and an Approved Supplier is selected, a Purchase Order is issued for the calculated quantity. It is traceable to the Replenishment Signal and the Supply Agreement, so every replenishment decision is checked against inventory policy.

Name: Strategic Sourcing
Documentation:
**New spend starts a sourcing cycle.** When spend in a category crosses a threshold or a specification changes, Strategic Sourcing defines what the organisation needs and goes to market. Supplier candidates are evaluated against qualification criteria, proposals are compared, and terms are negotiated before any commitment is made. The result is an Approved Supplier List and signed contracts that hold for multiple periods.

**Spending data and performance shape choices.** Strategic Sourcing depends on Category Spend Analysis to know where money goes, on Sourcing Requirements to define what to buy, and on Supplier Performance Reports to judge current suppliers. It produces Supply Agreements and Approved Supplier List updates that every later purchase uses. If performance breaches a threshold, it issues a Supplier Disqualification Notice and removes the supplier.

**A signed Supply Agreement locks terms.** When negotiation concludes and terms are approved, the Supply Agreement is issued. It commits the organisation to prices, volumes, and delivery conditions for a defined period. Every later Purchase Order in that category is issued against it, so the agreement is the contract that makes all subsequent purchasing possible.

Name: Tax Accounting
Documentation:
**A tax period closes.** Transaction Records from the period sit in the ledger, waiting to be classified. Tax Accounting calculates, records and reports the tax obligations those transactions create, and it files the result on time. The work is not optional: late or incorrect filings bring penalty and interest, and they misstate the financial statements.

**It converts ledger entries into filings.** The capability receives Transaction Record from all financial postings, Tax Rule from tax authorities, and Period Ledger at period close. It applies the rules in effect for that period, classifies each record, calculates the liability, and reconciles the ledger before producing a Tax Filing. When an audit question arrives, it handles the query; when a prior filing is wrong, it amends it.

**A Tax Filing lands each period.** It is issued each tax period with a Tax Calculation as supporting detail, and every tax position taken has a documented basis in the Tax Rules for the period. A Tax Payment Request follows when payment is due.

Name: D Deliver
Documentation:
**Customer Orders and return requests arrive.** A released Customer Order triggers allocation of stock, planning of delivery, and shipment to the customer's delivery point. A Return Request triggers evaluation of eligibility, authorization or refusal, and planning of the return movement. The work carries these movements from the moment a Customer Order is released for fulfilment until the Shipment is delivered and evidenced, and from a Return Request received until the returned items are physically received and their disposition is assigned. When it works, customers receive goods on time and return credits are not delayed.

**Outbound and inbound streams connect.** A Customer Order produces a Shipment, and every Shipment must depart with complete documentation. A Return Request yields a Return Authorization or a refusal, and a Shipping Schedule consolidates Shipments and sequences loading. These streams share one constraint: every delivery and return movement must be evidenced by a transfer of responsibility, such as a signature, an electronic handover, or an acceptance record.

**Acknowledged receipt ends liability.** A **Proof of Delivery** is issued when the receiving party confirms receipt, including condition and quantity. Without that evidence, custody and liability remain with the organisation even after the goods have left its premises.

Name: E Enable
Documentation:
**A contract comes up for renewal.** The organisation must decide whether to extend it, resolve any open claim against it, and show the decision rests on evidence. The Enable domain holds the commercial, contractual and compliance relationships with trading partners. It keeps every Contract current and lawful, resolves every Claim and Inquiry within its commitment window, and produces the evidence behind performance scores, risk positions and tax obligations. Without that evidence, there is no binding basis to transact and no defence for the actions taken.

**It turns demands into evidence-bound outputs.** Contract Proposals, Renewal Requests, Claims, Inquiries, Performance Data, Risk Events, Compliance Obligations, Sustainability Data and Transaction Records all arrive here, each logged and assessed before anything leaves. What leaves are Contracts, Renewal Agreements, Claim Decisions, Inquiry Responses, Performance Scorecards, Risk Registers, Compliance Reports, Sustainability Reports and Tax Filings, each issued only when its defined condition is met. These are the documents the rest of the organisation relies on to act lawfully.

**A Performance Scorecard closes the period.** It is issued at period close and records that performance against targets was monitored with evidence, not assumed. That single artefact shows the domain's rule in practice: every decision, approval and report must trace back to a Contract, a Compliance Obligation, a Risk Assessment or a Tax Rule.

Name: M Make
Documentation:
**A Production Schedule arrives.** Work begins. The Make function releases Work Orders against that schedule and controls the transformation sequence, material consumption, and quality evidence for every lot produced. It tracks every Work Order from release to completion and checks the accuracy of the Material Consumption Record, Capacity Usage Record, and Quality Record attached to each output. When it works, the output matches the accepted Product Specification and is ready for staging or stock posting at the promised time and cost.

**It depends on precise inputs.** The Production Schedule gives the authority for what to produce and when; the Product Specification gives the approved product definition, routing, and acceptance criteria. Material Availability and the Capacity Plan tell the function whether the inputs and time exist to run a Work Order. The Quality Standard sets the acceptance threshold each lot meets. Its outputs feed the next stage with a Completed Work Order and a Finished Good Receipt, along with the material, capacity, and quality records that make each lot traceable.

**The Completed Work Order closes.** It is issued only when every operation is recorded, all material issued, and the Quality Record for the lot is accepted. No Work Order completes until its last required operation is recorded and its Quality Record closes.

Name: P Plan
Documentation:
**Expected work becomes agreed work.** The planning function turns demand expectations and capacity constraints into executable plans that allocate resources, funds, and schedules across the organisation. It resolves conflicts between what is expected and what is possible, then issues the plans that guide acquisition, production, delivery, and return. Forecast error, capacity utilisation, and the timeliness of plan publication are the measures it is held to.

**Reality updates the plan.** A Demand Signal changes the forecast; a Customer Order feeds demand aggregation; a Return Request triggers reverse flow planning; a Supplier Invoice enters cost and payment planning; a Performance Report adjusts lead times and capacity assumptions. Each of those inputs is checked for completeness and authority before it is allowed to influence a plan. The function holds no authority to change demand or capacity directly, so it works through the plans themselves.

**One plan binds all commitments.** When every constituent part agrees, the **Integrated Supply Chain Plan** is issued. That is the point where purchase, production, delivery, and financial intentions stop competing and become one reconciled schedule, published in time to direct the next cycle of work.

Name: S Source
Documentation:
**A demand signal starts the check.** When a demand or replenishment signal arrives, the first job is to see whether an existing Supply Agreement covers it. If one does, the work moves to issuing a Purchase Order or adjusting a schedule. If not, the requirement goes through validation and supplier qualification before anything is committed. This keeps purchasing inside agreed terms for cost, quality, and delivery timing, and it protects supply continuity.

**Three connections keep purchases honest.**
- Supplier Performance Reports update ratings and trigger Corrective Action Requests.
- Return Requests are only authorised when they match the original Purchase Order and contract return terms.
- Supplier Invoices are matched against Purchase Orders and Goods Receipts before payment.

These connections tie every acquisition to evidence and contract, so suppliers stay accountable and returns stay recoverable.

**A Purchase Order fixes the commitment.** When a valid requirement matches an Approved Supplier with an active Supply Agreement, a Purchase Order is issued. It records what will be bought, at what price, and by when. That single record is the point where a need becomes a promise, and suppliers hold the organisation to it.

Name: Value Streams
Documentation: **A category of end-to-end flows.** This grouping organises the value streams that describe how work moves from customer need to fulfilled demand. Process designers and business architects define these flows to show the sequence of activities, the roles involved, and the information and materials that pass between them. Leaders and improvement teams rely on value streams to identify waste, measure lead time, and align cross-functional efforts. They provide a holistic view of value creation, linking planning, sourcing, making, and delivering into a coherent whole.

Name: Business Objects
Documentation: **A collection of supply chain records.** The Business Objects grouping encompasses the information artefacts created and used across all supply chain processes. These objects hold data, state, and status that describe what is planned, sourced, made, delivered, and enabled. Planners, buyers, makers, deliverers, and enablers create and update these records as work progresses. All supply chain actors rely on them to coordinate activities, make decisions, and keep a consistent record of what has happened, what is happening, and what is expected next.

Name: Approvals, Decisions & Solutions
Documentation: **A category of decision records.** This grouping brings together the business objects that capture authorisations, choices, and resolutions made during supply chain planning and execution. Planners and managers create these objects to record what was approved, decided, or solved. Execution teams, auditors, and other stakeholders rely on them to act consistently, verify what was agreed, and maintain accountability across the organisation.

Name: Commercial Documents
Documentation: **A category of trade documents.** This grouping holds the commercial documents that formalise buying and selling relationships and transactions. Procurement and sales teams create these documents when they negotiate terms, issue orders, or confirm agreements. Suppliers, customers, and finance teams rely on them to verify obligations, process payments, and resolve disputes. These records capture the binding details of commercial activity, including quantities, prices, delivery terms, and conditions, so that all parties work from the same agreed information.

Name: Generic Signals / Data
Documentation: **A category of operational data.** This grouping brings together the generic signals and data points that reflect the current state of supply chain activity. Systems, sensors, and operational teams create these signals as work happens, capturing events, measurements, and status changes. Planners, monitors, and automated decision processes rely on this data to detect conditions, trigger actions, and inform real-time adjustments. The records are less formal than documents but essential for visibility and responsiveness across the chain.

Name: Inventory & Materials
Documentation: **A category of stock records.** This grouping holds the business objects that track inventory levels, material specifications, and movement of goods. Warehouse, production, and procurement teams create and update these records when materials are received, consumed, moved, or counted. Planners, makers, and logistics teams rely on them to know what is available, where it is located, and how much is committed. These records support decisions on replenishment, production scheduling, and fulfilment, ensuring that supply matches demand.

Name: Logistics & Shipping Documents
Documentation: **A category of shipping paperwork.** This grouping contains the documents that accompany and control the movement of goods across the supply chain. Shippers, carriers, and receiving teams create these records when goods are dispatched, transported, and delivered. They provide proof of shipment, instructions for handling, and details for customs and payment. Logistics coordinators, warehouse staff, and finance teams rely on them to track shipments, verify receipt, and settle transportation charges. These documents ensure that goods move through the network with a clear chain of custody and accountability.

Name: Performance & Risk Artifacts
Documentation: **A category of assessment records.** This grouping holds the artefacts that capture performance results and risk evaluations. Risk managers and performance analysts create these records when they review operations, conduct audits, or assess potential disruptions. They include scorecards, risk registers, and analysis reports that summarise findings and recommended actions. Leadership, auditors, and improvement teams rely on them to understand current capability, exposure, and compliance. These artefacts support governance by providing evidence of what is working well and where intervention is needed.

Name: Planning & Forecasting Artifacts
Documentation: **A category of forward-looking plans.** This grouping brings together the artefacts used for planning and forecasting supply chain activity. Planners create these records to project demand, outline supply responses, and schedule resources. They include demand plans, supply plans, and production schedules that translate strategy into operational targets. Execution teams, procurement, and production rely on them to align their work with expected needs. These artefacts are updated as new information arrives, enabling the organisation to adapt to changes and maintain balance between supply and demand.

Name: Reference & Master Data
Documentation: **A category of foundational data.** This grouping holds the reference and master data that define the stable entities used across the supply chain. Data stewards and administrators create and maintain these records for products, locations, suppliers, customers, and other core objects. They provide consistent identifiers, attributes, and hierarchies that all other business objects rely on for accuracy. Planners, buyers, makers, and deliverers use this data to avoid duplication, ensure correct transactions, and analyse performance. It is the single source of truth for describing the organisation's operational landscape.

Name: Requests & Inquiries
Documentation: **A category of inbound asks.** This grouping brings together the requests and inquiries that arrive from customers, suppliers, and internal parties. These records capture a need for information, a quote, a service, or a specific action. Requesters create them to initiate a process, and responsive teams use them to prioritise and track fulfilment. Customer service, sales, procurement, and support teams rely on these objects to ensure that each inquiry is acknowledged, answered, and closed in a timely and consistent manner.

Name: Returns & Claims
Documentation: **A category of reverse flow records.** This grouping holds the business objects that manage returned goods and claims for defects, shortages, or damages. Customers, suppliers, and receiving teams create these records when a return is requested or a claim is filed. They capture the reason, condition, and resolution of the issue. Service, quality, and finance teams rely on them to process refunds, replacements, or repairs, and to identify recurring problems. These records support customer satisfaction and drive corrective actions in the supply chain.

Name: Strategy & Network Design
Documentation: **A category of strategic artefacts.** This grouping brings together the records used for long-term supply chain strategy and network design. Executive planners and analysts create these artefacts when they evaluate network configurations, capacity investments, and sourcing strategies. They include models, scenarios, and decision papers that compare options and recommend structural changes. Leadership teams rely on them to make informed choices about where to locate facilities, how to allocate resources, and how to shape the supply chain for future resilience and efficiency.

Name: Metrics
Documentation: **A category of performance measures.** This grouping brings together the metrics used to assess supply chain performance. Analysts and managers define these measurements to track cost, service, quality, speed, and other outcomes. They are calculated from operational data and business objects, then reported to decision makers. Executives, process owners, and improvement teams rely on metrics to compare actual performance against targets, identify gaps, and prioritise corrective actions. These measures provide a consistent basis for evaluating how well the supply chain delivers value.

Name: Adaptability
Documentation: **A group of supply chain performance measures.** It gathers metrics that track how quickly and effectively the supply chain adjusts to changes in demand, supply, or operating conditions. Managers use these metrics to assess flexibility and to guide decisions on capacity, sourcing, and process changes. The model groups them separately to highlight the supply chain's ability to handle uncertainty and to balance adaptability against other metric groups such as cost and efficiency.

Name: Asset Efficiency
Documentation: **Measures of how well assets are used.** This group collects metrics that indicate the return on physical and financial assets employed in the supply chain, including inventory, facilities, and equipment. Planners and finance teams use these metrics to improve utilization and reduce waste. The model separates asset efficiency from other metric groups because it focuses on the productivity of resources rather than on speed, cost, or reliability, helping decision-makers see where capital is tied up and identify opportunities to free it.

Name: Cost
Documentation: **A category of supply chain cost metrics.** It includes measures that capture the expense of planning, sourcing, making, and delivering products and services. Cost metrics are used by management to control spending, set budgets, and evaluate trade-offs with service levels. The model groups cost measures together so that total supply chain cost can be tracked consistently and compared across different operating scenarios. This group sits alongside other metric groups, allowing leaders to balance cost against responsiveness, dependability, and other performance dimensions.

Name: Dependability
Documentation: **Measures of supply chain reliability.** This group gathers metrics that show whether orders are delivered on time, in full, and without errors. Operations and customer service teams use these metrics to monitor performance against promises and to identify where reliability fails. The model separates dependability from other metric groups because it reflects the supply chain's trustworthiness from a customer's perspective, and it is essential for maintaining service levels and long-term relationships.

Name: Key Risk
Documentation: **A collection of risk-related performance measures.** It includes metrics that assess exposure to supply chain disruptions, such as supplier failures, demand shocks, or logistics breakdowns. Risk managers and executives use these metrics to evaluate the likelihood and potential impact of adverse events and to plan mitigation actions. The model groups key risk metrics separately to keep risk visibility high and to support decisions about redundancy, insurance, and resilience investment, ensuring that risk is not hidden within other performance categories.

Name: Profitability
Documentation: **Measures of financial return from supply chain activities.** This group gathers metrics that link supply chain performance to profit, such as margin contribution, return on supply chain assets, and cost-to-serve. Finance and executive teams use these metrics to judge whether supply chain decisions create economic value. The model separates profitability from other metric groups to make the financial outcome of supply chain work explicit, enabling leaders to weigh profit against other objectives like sustainability or responsiveness.

Name: Responsiveness
Documentation: **A supply chain performance metric group.** Responsiveness collects the measures that show how quickly a supply chain detects and responds to changes in demand, supply, or operating conditions. It sits alongside other metric groups such as Dependability, Adaptability, Cost, Asset Efficiency, Sustainability, Key Risk, and Profitability in the Metrics category. The model uses this grouping to give planners and decision makers a single place to review time-related performance. The individual members of Responsiveness are the specific speed and reaction measurements that an organisation chooses to track.

Name: Sustainability
Documentation: **Measures of environmental and social performance.** This group collects metrics on the supply chain's impact on the environment, such as carbon emissions, waste, water use, and labor practices. Sustainability teams and corporate leadership use these metrics to meet compliance obligations, reduce footprint, and improve reputation. The model groups sustainability metrics separately to ensure they receive focused attention alongside traditional performance dimensions like cost and profitability, supporting balanced decision-making.

Name: Acquire-to-Retire
Documentation: **Tracks an asset through its useful life.** The Acquire-to-Retire value stream covers the full lifecycle of an asset from acquisition through operation and maintenance to retirement or disposal. It is used by asset managers, finance teams, and operational staff to ensure assets are acquired, recorded, depreciated, maintained, and ultimately disposed of in a controlled manner. This supports decisions on capital investment, maintenance planning, and asset utilization, providing a complete view of asset performance and cost from purchase to end of life.

Name: Forecast-to-Plan
Documentation: **An end-to-end planning value stream.** It turns demand forecasts and financial forecasts into coordinated plans for budgeting, sourcing, production, and delivery. Business planners and finance teams execute this stream to produce aligned plans, while leaders rely on it to set operational targets and allocate resources. The stream serves the work of planning finance, supply chain operations, demand forecasting, budgeting, sourcing, making, and delivering, as well as financial forecasting.

Name: Hire-to-Retire
Documentation: **Manages the employee lifecycle from hire to exit.** Hire-to-Retire covers all human resources processes from recruiting and onboarding through development, performance management, and eventual retirement or separation. It is used by HR professionals and line managers to manage workforce data, compensation, benefits, and compliance. The value stream supports decisions on talent acquisition, retention, and workforce planning, ensuring the organization has the right people with the right skills at the right time.

Name: Inquiry-to-Order
Documentation: **Converts customer inquiries into confirmed orders.** Inquiry-to-Order manages the sales process from initial customer inquiry through proposal, negotiation, and contract signing to order placement. It is used by sales teams, contract managers, and legal staff to track opportunities, develop proposals, obtain approvals, and finalize agreements. The value stream supports decisions on pricing, terms, and resource allocation for proposals, helping the organization win business and convert interest into revenue.

Name: Order-to-Cash
Documentation: **Fulfills customer orders and collects payment.** Order-to-Cash covers the entire process from receiving a customer order through delivery and invoicing to payment receipt. It is used by sales, operations, logistics, and finance teams to manage order validation, inventory allocation, shipping, and accounts receivable. The value stream supports decisions on order promising, delivery scheduling, and credit management, ensuring timely fulfillment and cash collection to maintain liquidity and customer satisfaction.

Name: Plan-to-Move
Documentation: **Plans the movement of goods across the supply chain.** Plan-to-Move focuses on planning transportation and logistics activities to ensure efficient movement of materials and products between locations. It is used by logistics planners, transportation managers, and warehouse supervisors to optimize routing, scheduling, and carrier selection. The value stream supports decisions on shipping modes, load consolidation, and inventory transfer, enabling cost-effective and timely delivery while maintaining supply chain visibility and control.

Name: Procure-to-Pay
Documentation: **Purchases goods and services and pays suppliers.** Procure-to-Pay covers the operational procurement cycle from purchase requisition through ordering, receiving, and invoice payment. It is used by procurement staff, requesters, receiving teams, and accounts payable to execute purchases, manage purchase orders, and ensure timely supplier payment. The value stream supports decisions on purchasing compliance, spend management, and cash flow, providing control over indirect and direct procurement activities.

Name: Record-to-Report
Documentation: **Records financial transactions and produces reports.** Record-to-Report captures all financial transactions from operational activities and consolidates them into financial statements and management reports. It is used by accountants, controllers, and financial analysts to ensure accurate bookkeeping, period-end closing, and regulatory reporting. The value stream supports decisions on financial performance, compliance, and strategic planning by providing a complete and reliable view of the organization's financial position.

Name: Source-to-Pay
Documentation: **Sources suppliers and manages procurement to payment.** Source-to-Pay encompasses the entire procurement process from strategic sourcing and supplier management through contracting, purchasing, and payment. It is used by procurement professionals, category managers, and accounts payable to select suppliers, negotiate contracts, execute purchases, and process invoices. The value stream supports decisions on supplier selection, contract terms, and spend optimization, driving cost savings and supplier performance across the organization.
